power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: Background Genomic surveillance of respiratory viruses typically relies on sequences from individuals seeking health care, and whether these sequences represent the viruses circulating in the community is not well-characterized.
We aimed to compare the diversity, proportion, and dynamics of influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 between clinical and community samples.

In this retrospective comparative genomic analysis, we used whole-genome sequences from community-based surveillance studies in the Seattle area, and clinical sequences from the Washington State Department of Health.
We compared clade proportions and dynamics, sequence-cluster diversity, non-synonymous mutations, and Ct values between clinical and community samples.
Viral whole genome sequencing (WGS) has transformed infectious disease surveillance and outbreak response over the past decade 1, 2 .
text.formatted: Viral whole genome sequencing (WGS) has transformed infectious disease surveillance and outbreak response over the past decade <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: The ability to rapidly characterize pathogen genetic diversity provides critical insights for public health decision-making, such as tracking transmission chains during outbreaks, identifying emerging variants and monitoring antimicrobial resistance 3 .
text.formatted: The ability to rapidly characterize pathogen genetic diversity provides critical insights for public health decision-making, such as tracking transmission chains during outbreaks, identifying emerging variants and monitoring antimicrobial resistance <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Genomic data now routinely complement traditional epidemiological approaches, enabling higher-resolution understanding of disease dynamics than was previously possible with phenotypic or partial gene sequencing methods alone 4.
text.formatted: Genomic data now routinely complement traditional epidemiological approaches, enabling higher-resolution understanding of disease dynamics than was previously possible with phenotypic or partial gene sequencing methods alone <ref type="bibr">4</ref>.

text.text: The COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed an unprecedented expansion of pathogen genomic surveillance infrastructure globally 5 .
text.formatted: The COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed an unprecedented expansion of pathogen genomic surveillance infrastructure globally <ref type="bibr">5</ref> .

text.text: In the United States, initiatives like the CDC's Baseline and National SARS-CoV-2 Strain Surveillance programs, combined with substantial investments in state and local public health laboratory infrastructure created and expanded sequencing capabilities across the country allowing genomes to be rapidly shared through public repositories like NCBI GenBank 6 .
text.formatted: In the United States, initiatives like the CDC's Baseline and National SARS-CoV-2 Strain Surveillance programs, combined with substantial investments in state and local public health laboratory infrastructure created and expanded sequencing capabilities across the country allowing genomes to be rapidly shared through public repositories like NCBI GenBank <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: This infrastructure has enabled extension of routine genomic surveillance to other respiratory pathogens of public health importance, particularly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza (flu) virus 7 .
text.formatted: This infrastructure has enabled extension of routine genomic surveillance to other respiratory pathogens of public health importance, particularly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza (flu) virus <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">7</ref> .

text.text: These three pathogens represent the major viral causes of acute respiratory illness and collectively impose substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden, especially in the elderly and immunocompromised 8, 9 .
text.formatted: These three pathogens represent the major viral causes of acute respiratory illness and collectively impose substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden, especially in the elderly and immunocompromised <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">9</ref> .

text.text: In 2019, an estimated 33 million children younger than 5 years contracted RSV and over 101,000 children died due to RSV-associated causes 10 .
text.formatted: In 2019, an estimated 33 million children younger than 5 years contracted RSV and over 101,000 children died due to RSV-associated causes <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">10</ref> .

text.text: Influenza causes infections in 5-10% of adults and 20-30% of children 11 .
text.formatted: Influenza causes infections in 5-10% of adults and 20-30% of children <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">11</ref> .

text.text: RSV genomic surveillance has gained urgency following the licensure of RSV vaccines and monoclonal antibody prophylaxis, creating a need to monitor for immune escape variants 12.
text.formatted: RSV genomic surveillance has gained urgency following the licensure of RSV vaccines and monoclonal antibody prophylaxis, creating a need to monitor for immune escape variants <ref type="bibr">12</ref>.

text.text: Viral epidemiology requires population-level surveillance of viral strains, and multiple strategies for measuring the presence of different strains at scale have been utilized for respiratory viruses.
This includes sampling specific populations, such as hospitalized patients 13 , random sequencing of positive samples 14 , and sequencing of wastewater samples 15 .
text.formatted: This includes sampling specific populations, such as hospitalized patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">13</ref> , random sequencing of positive samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">14</ref> , and sequencing of wastewater samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">15</ref> .

text.text: Genomic epidemiology of respiratory viruses has identified developments that are crucial for public health responses, such as inter-continental transmission of new pathogenic SARS-CoV-2 variants, nearly complete replacement of RSV clades between seasons, and prediction of emerging variants of influenza virus [16] [17] [18].
text.formatted: Genomic epidemiology of respiratory viruses has identified developments that are crucial for public health responses, such as inter-continental transmission of new pathogenic SARS-CoV-2 variants, nearly complete replacement of RSV clades between seasons, and prediction of emerging variants of influenza virus <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[18]</ref>.

text.text: The COVID-19 pandemic was a unique period in which broad, community-level testing was widely available and samples from community members were routinely sent to laboratories for testing and sequencing.

As this community testing infrastructure has waned, laboratories generally no longer have access to community samples, and genomic surveillance now relies predominantly on specimens from individuals who present for clinical care.

Whether this clinical sampling frame is representative of the viruses circulating in the broader population remains unclear, mainly due to the lack of studies that track viral dynamics in both hospital and community settings 19 .
text.formatted: Whether this clinical sampling frame is representative of the viruses circulating in the broader population remains unclear, mainly due to the lack of studies that track viral dynamics in both hospital and community settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">19</ref> .

text.text: Past studies have utilized localized wastewater sampling followed by targeted clinical screening to contain SARS-CoV-2 outbreaks 20 , demonstrating that these data can be highly impactful.
text.formatted: Past studies have utilized localized wastewater sampling followed by targeted clinical screening to contain SARS-CoV-2 outbreaks <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">20</ref> , demonstrating that these data can be highly impactful.

text.text: Given the high cost of viral genomic surveillance and the reduced funding for the sequencing of respiratory viral isolates post-pandemic, public health agencies need data to decide how to judiciously apply limited resources for the measurement of respiratory virus transmission.

In this study, we analyzed the viral diversity of seasonal RSV and influenza virus strains and pandemic SARS-CoV-2 strains isolated from both community members and from individuals seeking healthcare in the same time frame and geographic location.

The overall diversity of SARS-CoV-2 clades differed between sampling modalities but remained similar for RSV and influenza virus, highlighting that pandemic-scale infections in hospitalized populations do not completely reflect the pattern in the community at large.
Measurement of the viral diversity over time revealed that intra-clade temporal dynamics also differ between clinical and community infections for SARS-CoV-2.

Finally, we found that for SARS-CoV-2, sampling from clinical specimens led to the identification of more diverse strains than sampling from the community, whereas RSV and influenza showed no significant difference.

Together, these results suggest that clinical sampling may adequately capture the diversity of seasonal respiratory viruses, but that during pandemic-level transmission, viral populations sampled in hospital settings can diverge from those circulating in the community.
Future surveillance programs should prioritize a diverse sampling strategy.

We conducted a retrospective comparative genomic analysis of three respiratory pathogens (SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza) using whole genome sequencing data from clinical and community surveillance sources in Washington state.
The study period spanned 2019 to 2022, encompassing multiple respiratory virus seasons and capturing periods of varying transmission intensity for each pathogen.

Sequences were classified into two surveillance categories based on the context of specimen collection: clinical surveillance, comprising specimens collected from individuals seeking medical care at healthcare facilities; and community surveillance, comprising specimens collected through population-based sampling programs that did not require participants to be seeking medical attention.
Sequences and metadata were derived from four main sources: the Seattle Flu Study, Seattle Coronavirus Assessment Network, Husky Coronavirus Testing, and publicly available sequences from Genbank.
The Seattle Flu Study (SFS) was a multi-arm surveillance study established in 2018 to characterize the genomic epidemiology of respiratory pathogens in the Puget Sound region 19 .
text.formatted: The Seattle Flu Study (SFS) was a multi-arm surveillance study established in 2018 to characterize the genomic epidemiology of respiratory pathogens in the Puget Sound region <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">19</ref> .

text.text: SFS enrolled participants through multiple community-based channels including kiosks at public venues (libraries, transit stations, community centers), home-based self-swab collection, and outreach at schools, workplaces, daycare centers, and homeless shelters.
In addition, the clinical arms enrolled individuals seeking care at four regional hospitals and multiple clinics.

For this analysis, SFS specimens collected during hospital-based care visits were classified as clinical, whereas specimens collected at outpatient clinics or kiosks set up within these locations (Sea Mar Community Health Centers, UW Hall Health, and Seattle Children's Hospital outpatient clinic) were classified as community samples.

Participants with symptoms associated with acute respiratory illness (ARI) provided nasal swabs specimens and linked information including demographics, symptoms/illness characteristics, and other metadata.
Specimens underwent multiplex RT-PCR testing for a panel of respiratory pathogens, with positive samples reflexed to whole genome sequencing for influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2.
The Seattle Coronavirus Assessment Network (SCAN) was launched in March 2020 as an extension of SFS infrastructure to enable population-based SARS-CoV-2 surveillance 21.
text.formatted: The Seattle Coronavirus Assessment Network (SCAN) was launched in March 2020 as an extension of SFS infrastructure to enable population-based SARS-CoV-2 surveillance <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">21</ref>.

text.text: SCAN utilized home-based self-collection of nasal swabs, with test kits distributed through mail, drive-through sites, and community partner locations.

The program was designed to capture SARS-CoV-2 infections across the community regardless of symptoms, testing access, or healthcare utilization, with enrollment open to all King County residents during the study period.
SCAN contributed RSV and influenza sequences from specimens tested on multiplex respiratory panels.
The Husky Coronavirus Testing (HCT) program 22 provided SARS-CoV-2 screening to students, staff, and faculty at the University of Washington from September 2020 to July 2023.
text.formatted: The Husky Coronavirus Testing (HCT) program <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">22</ref> provided SARS-CoV-2 screening to students, staff, and faculty at the University of Washington from September 2020 to July 2023.

text.text: Participants completed daily attestations via email or text message, and those reporting symptoms, recent travel, or exposure to a known SARS-CoV-2 case were offered SARS-CoV-2 testing.
Participants could also request testing for any reason in the absence of exposure or symptoms.
Participants self-collected nasal swabs at campus testing sites or returned them via campus drop-boxes or courier.

Samples were tested by PCR and SARS-CoV-2-positive specimens with Ct values under 30 underwent sequencing using a whole genome amplicon sequencing approach (Illumina COVIDSeq) as described previously 22 .
text.formatted: Samples were tested by PCR and SARS-CoV-2-positive specimens with Ct values under 30 underwent sequencing using a whole genome amplicon sequencing approach (Illumina COVIDSeq) as described previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">22</ref> .

text.text: HCT contributed SARS-CoV-2 sequences to the community surveillance arm of this study.
Together, these studies sampled infections across a spectrum of severity, including asymptomatic and mildly symptomatic cases that would not typically present to healthcare settings.
While the programs were concentrated in the Seattle metropolitan area, this geographic focus provides comparability with clinical surveillance data, which was also predominantly from this region.

text.text: The primary sources of clinical sequences included hospital-based diagnostic laboratories, commercial reference laboratories (e.g., LabCorp, Quest Diagnostics), and the University of Washington Clinical Virology Laboratory, which serves as a major reference laboratory for healthcare facilities throughout the Pacific Northwest.

Although the WA DOH surveillance system receives specimens from patients presenting to a range of healthcare settings, including emergency departments, inpatient hospital units, outpatient clinics, and urgent care facilities, the sequences provided by WA DOH for this analysis were specifically from individuals hospitalized as a result of SARS-CoV-2 infection, rather than from all individuals presenting for care.

Testing was performed for diagnostic purposes as part of routine clinical care, and specimens were subsequently sequenced through WA DOH's genomic surveillance program or sequencing efforts at submitting laboratories.

The selection of specimens for sequencing varied across the study period and across laboratories, and ranged from sequencing of all positive specimens, random sampling of positives, to targeted sequencing of specimens from hospitalized patients or suspected vaccine breakthrough cases.
Classification of sequences as clinical was performed using the Washington Disease Reporting System (WDRS), WA DOH's integrated disease surveillance platform.
Sequences were classified as clinical if they were linked to a diagnostic test ordered in the context of a healthcare encounter, as documented in WDRS.
No additional metadata on these samples was available.
Temporal matching between surveillance sources is critical for valid comparison, as pathogen diversity changes rapidly over time.
The study period was selected to maximize temporal overlap between community and clinical surveillance data sources while capturing sufficient genomic diversity for meaningful comparison.
For time-stratified analyses, we selected periods with at least 3 months of continuous detection in both surveillance sources.
For SARS-CoV-2, the study period of 2020 to 2022 encompasses multiple variant waves, including the emergence and spread of Delta (21J) and the Omicron sub-lineages BA.1 (21K) and BA.5 (22B).
The HCT program operated from September 2020 to September 2022, defining the window for community surveillance data availability.

For RSV and influenza, the study period of 2019 to 2021 encompasses two respiratory seasons (2019/2020 and 2020/2021), with influenza sequences derived from the 2019/2020 season only, with SFS/SCAN enrollment occurring throughout this period.
Specimens from community studies (SFS, SCAN, HCT) were processed and sequenced using standardized protocols within each program (see above).

Generally, respiratory specimens were tested by multiplex RT-PCR, and pathogen-positive specimens with cycle threshold (Ct) values below thresholds defined for the study or surveillance program were selected for whole genome sequencing.
Sequencing and genome assembly approaches depended on the study, timeperiod and submitting laboratory, and assembled genomes were deposited to NCBI Genbank.

text.text: This suggests that sampling hospitalized patients reveals greater genetic diversity than sampling pandemic viruses in the community, possibly because participants in community screening were more homogeneous in their exposures, and thus sampled fewer transmission chains, than individuals hospitalized for SARS-CoV-2 infection.

We then compared the abundance of non-synonymous amino acid mutations in flu, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 between clinical and community populations, as single substitutions can alter drug resistance or pathogenicity.

For RSV (Table S2), 37 non-synonymous mutations differed significantly in frequency between the two sources (n = 373 clinical and 165 community sequences; χ² test with Cramér's V = 0.13-0.32, all p adj < 0.05).

text.text: All 37 were in RSV-A and all were enriched in clinical samples, concentrated in the attachment glycoprotein G (15 mutations) and the polymerase L (14 mutations); the largest differences were at G:I265L (66.2% of clinical versus 31.5% of community sequences) and L:L1438Q (66.5% versus 32.7%; p adj = 4.7 × 10¹²).

For SARS-CoV-2 (Table S3), 80 mutations differed significantly between sources (n = 2,717 clinical and 5,907 community sequences; Cramér's V = 0.09-0.24, all p adj ≤ 2.0 × 10¹), but enrichment was bidirectional with 51 mutations more frequent in clinical samples and 29 in community samples.

text.text: The strongest clinical enrichments were S:L452R (43.6% versus 20.1%; Cramér's V = 0.24, p adj = 4.6 × 10¹¹¹), S:F486V (21.1% versus 6.2%) and M:D3N (18.4% versus 4.7%), whereas spike changes characteristic of Omicron BA.1, including S:Q493R (44.2% versus 66.6%), S:L212I and S:ins214EPE (both ~26% versus ~47%), were more frequent in community samples.

The bidirectional pattern for SARS-CoV-2 is consistent with the clade-composition differences described above, whereas the uniformly clinical enrichment in RSV-A was not accompanied by a detectable difference in clade proportions.
For flu, no mutations differed significantly in frequency between clinical and community sequences.

We extended this analysis by comparing the enrichment of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein mutations associated with monoclonal antibody resistance (Figure 5D; χ² test with Cramér's V = 0.11 -0.24, p = 4.55 x 10 -111 -2.22 x 10 -27 ).

text.text: We hypothesized that antiviral resistance mutations would be preferentially enriched in clinical isolates due to the higher usage of antivirals in this population.
Surprisingly, certain mutations (R346K, S371L, Q493R, G496S, N856K) were more prevalent in community samples.
These results demonstrate that clinically relevant mutations can be widespread in the community.

Given that clinically attended infections are more severe compared to infections in community members, we hypothesized that the C t value (inversely proportional to number of viral genome copies) in clinical samples would be lower than in community samples.

We compared the range of C t values per clade for the subset of sequenced samples where both the C t values and lineage assignments were available for flu (1462, 97%), RSV, (538, 100%), and SARS-CoV-2 We found that high-level viral diversity at the level of clades was significantly different between these two sources for SARS-CoV-2 isolates but not for RSV or flu.
This could be due to number of factors.

First, the transmission and spread of SARS-CoV-2 during our sampling period was a pandemic-level mass infection of a susceptible population while RSV transmission occurred in a seasonal, periodic manner in a population with some level of pre-existing immunity.
RSV transmission also occurred after suppression from the COVID-19 pandemic and before anti-RSV monoclonal antibodies were available.
Basic transmission differences such as the number of people being infected and those who are more likely to be severely infected, such as infants with RSV 28 , may factor into this difference.

text.text: RSV, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 are also genetically distinct viruses that replicate through different mechanisms.
Another contributing factor to this finding could be the unequal sampling between clinical and community sites, especially for the SARS-CoV-2 isolates 29 .

text.text: Oversampling certain groups, for example on college campuses, would yield more closely related viruses, underestimating community diversity and skewing community clade frequencies toward locally circulating strains.

Differences in sample size may also increase power to detect clade differences for SARS-CoV-2, and lower-viral-load community infections may be underrepresented among sequenced samples because sequencing success depends on viral load.
We hypothesized that severe infections would result in a bottleneck and therefore expected within-clade diversity to be lower in clinical samples.

However, rarefaction analysis of genomic clusters showed the opposite pattern for SARS-CoV-2, with clinical sequences more diverse than community sequences, and no clear difference between sources for RSV or flu.

One explanation for this may be that individuals hospitalized for SARS-CoV-2 infection were drawn from a broader cross-section of the population than participants in community testing programs, as noted above, and therefore captured a wider range of transmission chains.

Another is that clinical infections are associated with a higher viral load, which likely increases the intrapersonal diversity of viral strains in an individual and a greater composite divergence from the original infecting strain.

Nosocomial spread of respiratory viruses is well-documented, and multiple studies have found direct lines of transmission of RSV and SARS-CoV-2 between patients using genomic analyses; however, such transmission would be expected to enrich a few outbreak strains and lower diversity, and WA DOH sequences came from individuals hospitalized because of SARS-CoV-2 infection rather than infected after admission. text.text: We therefore compared the frequency of individual non-synonymous substitutions, including mutations associated with monoclonal antibody resistance, between clinical and community sequences for each of the three viruses.
At this resolution the two sources also diverged, but not in the direction expected.

RSV showed non-synonymous mutations enriched in clinical sequences despite indistinguishable clade proportions, while SARS-CoV-2 showed differentially abundant mutations with enrichment in both directions, and no flu mutations differed significantly.

Several spike substitutions associated with monoclonal antibody resistance were in fact more prevalent in community samples, indicating that clinically relevant mutations circulate widely outside of care settings and may be detected late by clinical sampling alone.
This study has a number of limitations.

First, sampling differed markedly across programs in geography, demographics, symptom status, and specimen-selection criteria; although rarefaction addresses unequal depth through repeated sampling at sequential levels of observations, it cannot fully remove these other biases.
Second, the comparison rests on three viruses sampled in one region over a limited window, including the atypical pandemic period, which perturbed RSV seasonality and may limit generalizability.
Third, assembly and specimenselection methods varied among the laboratories contributing clinical sequences, which we mitigated with uniform quality filtering but could not fully standardize.
Fourth, Ct values were available for only a subset of specimens and are sensitive to sampling timing and swab type.
Fifth, the level of sequences available for each virus differed greatly.
This can inflate the power of analyses used here and confounds direct comparisons between each virus.

Sixth, clade definitions differ in granularity across the three viruses: the Nextclade nomenclature for SARS-CoV-2 partitions diversity into more, finer-scale clades than those currently defined for RSV and influenza, so more within-clade diversity is collapsed for the latter.
Finer partitioning increases the opportunity to detect differences in clade composition between sampling sources, which may partly contribute to the larger differences observed for SARS-CoV-2.
Our cluster-based rarefaction analysis, which uses a uniform SNP threshold independent of clade nomenclature, partially mitigates this concern.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates key differences in viral dynamics between clinical and community-based sampling and suggests that a combined approach is best for capturing both the breadth and depth of viral diversity.

DISCUSSION Respiratory virus surveillance often aims to identify new variants which may have increased drug resistance or pathogenicity.

Most sequences in public repositories, however, come from specimens collected when people seek medical care, as opposed to community-based programs that sample individuals irrespective of care-seeking.
It is unclear how well either source of sampling represents the true diversity of viruses circulating in a population.
In this work, we compared multiple levels of viral diversity between samples acquired from community and clinical sampling programs for RSV, flu, and SARS-CoV-2.
